title: Elderly Couple's Steel-Plate Paratha Meal on Flight Goes Viral, Reignites Homemade Food Debate
excerpt: A photo of an older couple eating chapatis, sabzi and Amul dahi from a steel thali mid-flight has drawn millions of views and mixed reactions — the latest in a string of viral Indian in-flight food moments.
body:
• A photo of an elderly couple eating homemade chapatis, sabzi and Amul dahi from a steel plate on a flight went viral after X user Nalini Unagar posted it on August 30.
  • The image is the latest in a series of viral Indian in-flight food moments, including a family of 15 that turned an IndiGo cabin into a mini cafeteria days earlier.
  • Reactions are sharply divided — supporters call it a stand against overpriced airline food, while critics question cabin etiquette and food safety at altitude.
  • Indian airlines generally permit passengers to carry solid homemade food on domestic flights.

An elderly couple sitting in their aircraft seats, calmly eating homemade chapatis, sabzi and curd from a steel plate, has become the internet's latest food debate. The image, posted on X by food content creator Nalini Unagar (@NalinisKitchen) on August 30, has drawn millions of views and thousands of comments within hours.

"If you are paying thousands for a flight ticket and still have to eat tasteless airline food, this is what you should do," Unagar wrote. "This uncle and aunty came prepared with their own homemade food and are enjoying it. I am lovin' it."

The couple had packed a full meal — chapatis with sabzi on a steel plate, alongside a packet of Amul dahi — the kind of practical, no-fuss travel meal that generations of Indian families have carried on trains, buses and now, increasingly, on flights.

A Growing Trend in Indian Skies

The viral photo arrives just days after another in-flight food moment dominated social media. On August 26, a video showed a family of roughly 15 passengers on an IndiGo flight unpacking boxes of theplas, dhoklas and samosas, distributing them on disposable plates and walking through the cabin to serve relatives seated across different rows.

That clip, posted by X user @choga_don, drew sharper criticism. "A North Indian family opened a cafeteria on a running flight," the caption read. While some users praised the family for cleaning up after themselves, others called it a breach of civic sense in a shared, enclosed space.

The elderly couple's quieter meal has attracted a warmer response, though the debate it sparked is essentially the same: Is carrying homemade food on a flight a harmless personal choice or a cabin etiquette issue?

The Case For and Against

Supporters argue the couple represents a practical, relatable response to airline food that is often bland, cold and overpriced. "Homemade food is best," one commenter wrote. Others drew parallels to Indian railway travel, where packed meals are a cultural institution. "It's right — even paying thousands of rupees for airlines that are providing tasteless food, they should allow us to get the home food to eat on the flight, like how we eat in trains," another wrote.

Critics raised a different set of concerns. Some pointed out that airline meals are designed with fewer spices to minimize discomfort at altitude, where low cabin pressure can temporarily dull taste and smell. Strong-smelling food in a pressurized cabin can linger for the entire flight, affecting passengers who did not choose it. "It's a flight, not a picnic spot," one user commented.

"If you are paying thousands for a flight ticket and still have to eat tasteless airline food, this is what you should do. This uncle and aunty came prepared with their own homemade food and are enjoying it."

— Nalini Unagar (@NalinisKitchen), X

What the Rules Actually Say

Indian airlines, including IndiGo, Air India and SpiceJet, generally allow passengers to carry solid homemade food on domestic flights. Liquids above 100 millilitres are restricted by security regulations, but items like chapatis, sandwiches, fruits and dry snacks are typically permitted. The steel plate and Amul dahi packet in the couple's meal fall within what most carriers allow.

The debate is less about rules and more about norms — an evolving negotiation between India's deeply rooted food culture and the etiquette expectations of modern air travel.

A Cultural Marker

For many Indians, the steel thali and packed parathas are not just food — they are a statement of identity. Decades of train travel built a tradition of elaborate packed meals, and the habit has followed passengers into aircraft cabins as air travel has become more accessible. India's domestic passenger numbers have grown steadily, with budget carriers like IndiGo bringing first-time flyers into the system at scale.

What the elderly couple likely saw as a simple, practical meal, the internet turned into a referendum on culture, class and cabin manners. The chapatis, at least, looked unfazed.
image_caption: An elderly couple eats homemade chapatis, sabzi and Amul dahi from a steel plate during a flight. The image, posted on X by Nalini Unagar on August 30, has gone viral with millions of views.
nri_angle: The viral moment reflects a deeply Indian travel tradition — packing ghar ka khana for every journey. For the diaspora, the steel thali and Amul dahi packet are instantly recognizable cultural markers, evoking memories of family trips and home-cooked meals that no airline menu can replace.
